1.pericope_label: So thou, O son of man, I have set thee a watchman unto the house of Israel; therefore thou shalt hear the word at my mouth, and warn them from me
debates: Whether the watchman is chosen by the people or appointed by God
Why the watchman charge is restated here after the earlier commission
Where the blame falls when the warned are taken
outliers: Keil and Delitzsch head the whole second half of the book as the announcement of salvation, against the judgments of the first half
Clarke marks the asymmetry that here the people choose the watchman while in the earlier commission the Lord appoints him
Henry holds that Israel did not set its own watchman, being less wise for their souls than for their temporal interests, so God appointed one for them
Ellicott gives the section a retrospective purpose, explaining why the prophet had until then spoken so much of judgment
themes: A sentinel giving the alarm by discharging a gun
A man who ignores the trumpet called his own murderer
Princes and statesmen named the watchmen of a kingdom
A passage said to be too clear to need comment

10.pericope_label: As I live, saith the Lord God, I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked; but that the wicked turn from his way and live
debates: Whether the word about pining away was spoken absolutely or conditionally
Who the speakers of the complaint are
Why the teaching of an earlier chapter is repeated here
outliers: Henry holds the saying was spoken conditionally to bring them to repentance and is thrown back as though it had been absolute
Ellicott marks the reversal, that the same people who refused to believe the warning now despair once it is fulfilled
Gill notes the speakers are called the children of the prophet people rather than the people of God, since the children of God could not say such a thing
Ellicott explains the repetition as guarding against misunderstanding about the basis of acceptance with God
themes: A word and an oath called two immutable things
Long prayers and fasting twice in the week set against devouring widows houses
Threatenings becoming a savour of life and promises a savour of death
A pledge restored before sunset as evidence of repentance

21.pericope_label: And it came to pass in the twelfth year of our captivity, in the tenth month, in the fifth day of the month, that one that had escaped out of Jerusalem came unto me, saying, The city is smitten
debates: Whether the date is the eleventh year or the twelfth
Why the news took a year and five months to arrive
Whether the prophet had been wholly dumb until now
outliers: Clarke reports seven manuscripts collated by Kennicott, one of De Rossi and the Syriac reading the eleventh year, and thinks the shorter interval probably genuine
Ellicott defends the twelfth year by the logistics of the deportation, the halt at Riblah and the slow journey of captives carrying spoil
Wesley insists the prophet was not wholly dumb before, having prophesied against many nations, but was forbidden to speak of the Jews
Keil and Delitzsch take the date as marking the exact point at which the earlier promise was fulfilled and the restraint removed
themes: A fugitive who could say he had seen those scenes himself
Returning captives timed at exactly four months on the same road
A first word after the news that rebukes rather than consoles
A prophet vindicated by the event against those who contradicted him

23.pericope_label: Son of man, they that inhabit those wastes of the land of Israel speak, saying, Abraham was one, and he inherited the land: but we are many; the land is given us for inheritance
debates: Who the inhabitants of the wastes are
What standing upon the sword means
Why the land was to be left wholly uninhabited
outliers: Ellicott identifies the speakers as the poor left as vine-dressers together with Jews returning from Moab and Ammon, and dates the oracle before the murder of the governor
Ellicott denies that standing upon the sword can mean war here and takes it of individual crimes of violence
Ellicott contrasts Judah with the northern kingdom, whose land was repopulated by colonies because the ten tribes were not to return
Ellicott notes that from here to the closing vision none of the prophecies are dated, and they must span more than twelve years
themes: A claim that the promise is held better by the many than by the one
A retreat from one shelter to the next as each is taken away
Abraham said not to have owned one foot of the land
Natural fastnesses read for the forts of the English

30.pericope_label: And, lo, thou art unto them as a very lovely song of one that hath a pleasant voice, and can play well on an instrument: for they hear thy words, but they do them not
debates: Whether the people talk against the prophet or merely about him
Who the hearers in this closing section are
What the recognition at the end amounts to
outliers: Clarke follows two ancient versions in rendering the preposition concerning rather than against, since the following verses show the prophet was much respected
Ellicott agrees and reads the people as enjoying the eloquence of the prophet rather than opposing him, much as a popular preacher is treated now
Henry reads the same talk as invidious reflection behind the back of one they flattered to his face
Ellicott suggests the hearers are fresh captives of a worse moral character rather than those long with the prophet
themes: Talking at doorways called the custom of idle people in every country
A sermon heard as one hears a concert
Love shown only from the teeth outward
A recognition that arrives too late to profit by
